podcast.body: Her first record, a rewrite of Thomas Dorsey's "Hide Me and Vibosum." Tharp changed "singing" to "swinging" in the lyrics, and the song is often noted for having a potential double entendre, suggesting more worldly matters than Dorsey's original intent, which likely influenced the decision to make it her debut single. "Her arrangement largely stuck to Dorsey's original, with one important exception, where he had written singing, Tharp sang, Swinging."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This was Sister Rosetta Tharp's first single, released when she was 23 years old. She was known for combining electric guitar and gospel music in the 1930s and 1940s. Her pioneering work in melding religion and popular music is considered foundational to the story of rock and roll. "We just can't tell the story of Rock and Roll without Sister Rosetta Tharp."

srcs.episode: Ep. 32 - Take Me to Church - Religion in 70s Popular Music

podcast.body: This remake showcased a significant artistic improvement in Tharp's guitar playing, three years after her initial recording. It highlights her transition to electric guitar and her development of a distinctive single-note lead style. "Her remake of Rock Me, with Melinda's band from 1941, shows just how much her artistry had improved in just three years."
